B7C8.q: In Book VII, Chapter 8, how does Aristotle address the question of whether matter or form is more properly the substance of a sensible thing?
options: Matter is clearly the primary substance since it is the unchanging substratum underlying all changes
Form is the primary substance because it is the actualizing principle that makes matter into a determinate thing; matter alone is only potentially a thing
Matter and form are equally substances with no priority of one over the other
Neither matter nor form is substance; only the composite of both can be called a substance
B7C8.explanation: Aristotle argues that form, not matter, is more truly the substance of a sensible thing because form actualizes matter and gives it determinate being. Matter alone is only potential; it is form that makes a thing to be what it is.

B7C8.q: According to Aristotle, what is the relationship between the definition of a thing and the form of that thing?
options: The definition expresses the matter, not the form, so studying definitions is irrelevant to understanding form
The definition expresses the form—the essence or actualized structure—not the material composition; thus knowing the definition is knowing the form
The definition and form are unrelated concepts, one linguistic and one physical
The definition applies only to abstract objects like numbers, not to sensible substances
B7C8.explanation: Aristotle emphasizes that the definition of something expresses its form or essence, not the matter out of which it is made. The definition tells us what the thing is, which is precisely what the form is.

B7C8.q: Why does Aristotle argue that a definition cannot be an account of matter plus form, but must express form alone?
options: Because matter is entirely unknowable and cannot be included in any rational account

Because definition expresses what a thing is per se—its essence—and matter is not part of the essence but an external element; the definition must give the form, which unites and actualizes the matter
Because the form is unchanging while matter is always changing, making matter impossible to define
Because Aristotle believes sensible things have no matter, only form
B7C8.explanation: Aristotle holds that definition expresses the essential nature (form) of a thing, not its material composition. Matter is not part of the essence; the form is what makes a thing essentially what it is.

B7C9.q: In Chapter 9, how does Aristotle handle the puzzle of whether universals (like 'human-ness' or 'animal-ness') can be substances?
options: He concludes that universals are fully substances, existing separately from particulars, as Plato argued

He argues that universals cannot be primary substances because a substance must be a determinate individual ('this man'), whereas a universal is common to many; only particulars are primary substances
He shows that both universals and particulars are equally substances with no distinction between them
He claims universals are substances only in the realm of mathematics, not in the physical world
B7C9.explanation: Aristotle contends that while universals are real, they cannot be substances in the primary sense because substance is 'a this'—a determinate particular. Universals are common to many, so they lack the particularity required for primary substantiality.

B7C9.q: What does Aristotle mean by saying that form, though universal in character, exists actually only in particulars?
options: Form is never universal but always particular, so the statement is contradictory
Form has a universal nature (it applies to all members of a species) but its actual existence is always in determinate particulars; the universal is potential in each particular that exemplifies it
All particulars are illusions; only the universal form truly exists
Form exists universally in an abstract realm separate from any particulars
B7C9.explanation: Aristotle argues that form, though universal in that the same form defines many particulars (all individual humans share the form of humanity), exists actually only in determinate particular things. The universal exists as actual in each particular that possesses it.

B7C9.q: According to Aristotle's analysis in Chapter 9, why must there be generated substances (things that come into being) as well as eternal substances?
options: Because motion is impossible unless there are substances that undergo change, so eternal unchanging substances cannot account for all reality
Because the world requires both eternal substances (like the celestial spheres) and generated substances (like animals and plants) to explain the full diversity of being observed in nature
Because Aristotle rejects the existence of eternal substances altogether, making generation the only mode of coming-to-be
Because the form of generated things requires eternal matter as its substrate
B7C9.explanation: Aristotle posits both eternal and generated substances to account for all reality: some substances (like the heavens and divine intellect) are eternal and unchanging, while others (like animals and plants) come into being and perish, giving a complete account of nature.

B7C10.q: In Book VII, Chapter 10, what is Aristotle's main argument regarding the priority of form over matter in the order of causation?
options: Matter is prior because it is the substratum of all causation

Form is prior in the order of efficient cause (the agent that brings form about), of final cause (what the form aims at), and of knowledge (we know things through their form); hence form is more a principle or element than matter
Neither form nor matter has priority; they are equally causal
Matter is prior in the order of knowledge, but form is prior in the order of being
B7C10.explanation: Aristotle argues that form is prior to matter in multiple respects: as efficient cause (the agent actively produces form), as final cause (the end toward which generation aims), and as the principle of knowledge and intelligibility.

B7C10.q: How does Aristotle use the example of a syllable to illustrate the relationship between parts (material components) and the whole (the form)?
options: A syllable is identical to the sum of its letters, so parts and whole are the same

A syllable is not merely the letters joined together but requires a specific arrangement and unification; similarly, a substance is not just matter and parts but requires form to unify them into a single whole
Letters have no relation to syllables, which are purely abstract linguistic units
The whole syllable is less real than its individual letter-parts
B7C10.explanation: Aristotle uses the syllable example to show that while BA consists of B and A, a syllable is not merely the letters as a heap but requires a specific arrangement and unification. Similarly, form unifies matter's parts into a genuine whole.

B7C10.q: What distinction does Aristotle draw between calling something 'composed of' material elements versus 'composed of' form and matter as principles?
options: There is no meaningful distinction; composition is composition regardless of whether one discusses materials or principles
Things composed of material elements (bronze, wood) differ from things composed of form/matter principles in that the latter have a true substantial unity while the former are mere aggregates
Material composition applies only to artifacts like beds, while form/matter composition applies only to living things
Aristotle abandons the concept of material composition entirely in favor of form/matter language
B7C10.explanation: Aristotle distinguishes between discussing material constituents (bronze, wood) and discussing the form/matter principles that constitute a substance. Form and matter together constitute a true substantial unity, not a mere collection of material parts.

B7C11.q: In Chapter 11, how does Aristotle refute the view that substance might be composed of substances (i.e., that form and matter are both substances)?
options: He accepts the view as entirely coherent and necessary

He argues that if both form and matter were substances (primary beings in their own right), then a composite would be composed of substances, making substance divisible into substances; but the properties of the composite would be different from those of its components, which is impossible if both are substances
He claims form and matter are never distinct in any sensible thing
He argues that only form is a substance, while matter is purely non-being
B7C11.explanation: Aristotle's key point is that the properties of the composite differ from those of its material and formal components, which would be impossible if both form and matter were substances. Hence the composite substance cannot be composed of substances.

B7C11.q: What does Aristotle conclude about the relationship between a thing's parts and its definition?
options: A definition must include a list of all the physical parts of a thing
The parts into which a substance is divided enter into its definition, though not all parts—only those that are formal, not material; the material parts are external to the essential definition
Definitions have nothing to do with parts; they describe only abstract properties
All parts of a thing are equally essential to its definition
B7C11.explanation: Aristotle distinguishes between material parts (which vary and are external to essence) and formal parts (which express the structure of the form). Only formal parts enter into the definition, since the definition expresses the form's structure, not material composition.

B7C11.q: According to Aristotle, why are elements (like earth, air, fire, water) not substances in the primary sense, even though they seem to be simpler and more fundamental than complex organisms?
options: Elements are purely abstract and have no physical reality

Elements are matter without form, hence mere potentiality; they are only principles or material constituents, not actual substances, whereas concrete particulars (this man, this horse) that possess form are actual substances
Elements are substances, but they are secondary to organisms
Aristotle contradicts himself by claiming elements are both substances and not substances
B7C11.explanation: Elements lack form and are therefore only potentially things; they exist as raw material awaiting actualization by form. Actual substances must be determinate actualities, which requires both form and the matter that form organizes.

B7C12.q: In Book VII, Chapter 12, what is Aristotle's main concern in discussing whether substances come into being (are generated) or exist eternally?
options: He argues that all substances are eternal and never come into being

He asks whether the kinds (species) of substances come into being or pre-exist eternally, and argues that while particular individuals come into being, the forms/kinds persist eternally as the stable essences from which new individuals arise
He claims that nothing is eternal; all substances are generated and perish
He shows that the question is meaningless and cannot be answered
B7C12.explanation: Aristotle's concern is to understand how new substances come into being: individuals of a species come into being, but the species itself (the form, the essence) must pre-exist as an actualizing principle; hence forms or kinds are eternal principles from which generated individuals arise.

B7C12.q: How does Aristotle address the paradox that a thing must come from something like itself (since form produces form), yet this would require the form to exist before generation occurs?
options: He denies the premise entirely, saying unlike produces unlike in all cases

He argues that while the form must pre-exist in the agent (the parent or craftsman) that brings it about, it need not pre-exist in the generated thing itself; the form actualizes the matter into the same form that existed in the agent
He abandons the principle that like produces like as incoherent
He claims there is no such paradox and the form arises from pure non-being
B7C12.explanation: Aristotle resolves the apparent paradox by noting that form pre-exists in the efficient cause (parent or maker), not necessarily as a separate eternal principle; the agent actualizes the matter according to the form already present in itself.

B7C12.q: What does Aristotle conclude about the necessity of a first substance or first principle to ground the eternal recurrence of generated substances?
options: Generated substances alone are sufficient to explain their own perpetual re-creation without requiring any first principle
There must be an eternal substance that is the source of generation for all temporally generated things, otherwise generation itself would have no grounding in necessity, leaving all being contingent
First principles apply only to mathematics, not to physical substances
Aristotle rejects the notion of a first principle as inconsistent with his philosophy
B7C12.explanation: Aristotle argues that perpetual generation of temporally limited substances requires an eternal ground; otherwise, being would be entirely contingent. This points to the necessity of an eternal first substance (the unmoved mover) as the ultimate source of all becoming.

B7C13.q: In Chapter 13, how does Aristotle distinguish between the way form and matter enter into definition versus the way they enter into coming-to-be?
options: Form and matter are equally essential to both definition and generation

Definition expresses form alone (the essence), not matter; but in coming-to-be, matter is involved as the material cause that receives the form, making matter essential to generation but not to the essence expressed in definition
Matter enters into definition, while form is irrelevant to generation
Neither form nor matter has a role in either definition or generation
B7C13.explanation: Aristotle distinguishes between definition (which expresses form/essence alone) and generation (which requires both form and matter to be involved). Matter is the material cause of generation but is not part of the essential nature expressed in definition.

B7C13.q: What is Aristotle's response to the question of whether a definition can be circular—i.e., whether the parts of a definition must themselves be defined, leading to infinite regress?
options: He accepts infinite regress as inevitable and unavoidable in any system of definitions

He argues that an infinite regress in defining parts would make definition impossible, so there must be a stopping point; definitions are not circular but terminate in non-composite parts (unanalysable terms) that are primitive principles
He claims all definitions are circular and this poses no problem for knowledge
He shows that circular definitions are actually preferable to linear ones
B7C13.explanation: Aristotle argues against infinite regress in definition by holding that some terms are primitive and non-composite, serving as stopping points. A complete definition must terminate in such unanalysable terms.

B7C13.q: According to Aristotle, why is the form of a sensible substance not itself sensible or perceivable in the way that matter is?
options: Form is perceived through the senses just like matter

Form is the principle of intelligibility and organization that transcends sensibility; though we perceive individual sensible things (whose form gives them structure), the form itself is grasped by intellect through abstraction from sensible particulars, not by direct sensory perception
Sensible substances have no form, only matter
The form is sensible, but we can never perceive it due to our cognitive limitations
B7C13.explanation: Aristotle argues that form, though present in sensible things, is not itself a sensible object but an intelligible principle. We grasp form through intellect when we abstract from particular sensible instances.

B7C14.q: In Book VII, Chapter 14, what does Aristotle say about the relationship between definition and the parts that compose a definition?
options: A definition is identical to a random collection of words with no inner structure or unity
A definition has parts (the parts of the definition—genus, species, differentia), and these parts are unified by the form itself; the unity of a definition mirrors the unity that form gives to matter
Definitions cannot have parts; they are atomic units
The parts of a definition have no relationship to the thing being defined
B7C14.explanation: Aristotle draws a parallel between the unity of a substance (form unifying matter) and the unity of a definition (form unifying the definitional parts). The structure of a definition reflects the structure of the substance.

B7C14.q: How does Aristotle handle the question of whether specific differences (what distinguishes humans from other animals, for example) are substances or merely qualities?
options: Specific differences are purely accidental qualities with no essential role
Specific differences are part of the form itself and therefore part of the substance, though they are not themselves substances; they constitute the formal structure that makes a species what it is
Specific differences are independent substances equal in status to genera
Aristotle denies that any specific differences exist between kinds of things
B7C14.explanation: Aristotle treats specific differences (like 'rational' in rational animal) as formal determinations that constitute part of the essence, making them integral to substance even though they are not themselves substances.

B7C14.q: What is Aristotle's conclusion about whether the substance of a thing can be said to be composed of 'elements' in the way that syllables are composed of letters?
options: Substances are definitely composed of elements in the same way syllables are composed of letters

Substances are not composed of elements the way syllables are of letters; rather, form organizes matter into a determinate unity, whereas letters merely combine into a sequence; the analogy breaks down because a substance is a genuine unity, not a mere compound of separable parts
Syllables have nothing to do with letters; the analogy is pointless
Aristotle rejects both substances and syllables as real entities
B7C14.explanation: Aristotle notes that while we can talk of elements (material constituents), a substance is constituted by form organizing matter into a true unity, which is fundamentally different from letters combining into a sequence.

B7C15.q: In Chapter 15, what does Aristotle argue about the priority of being (ousia/substance) over the other categories (quality, quantity, relation, etc.)?
options: All categories are equally fundamental, with no priority among them

Substance is primary because all other categories (quality, quantity, relation) exist only in or relative to substance; quality is always the quality of something (a substance), quantity is the quantity of something, and so forth
Quality is the most fundamental category, with substance being derivative from it
The categories are not real features of being at all, merely linguistic distinctions
B7C15.explanation: Aristotle emphasizes that substance is the primary category because all other predicates presuppose substance: qualities, quantities, and relations all belong to substances. Remove substance and the others have no ground of being.

B7C15.q: According to Aristotle, why can't an accident (a non-substantial property like paleness or musical knowledge) be a substance?
options: Accidents are more real and eternal than substances

An accident is defined as something that 'is-not' a substance—it exists only in a substance and is predicated of a subject, never serving as the subject itself; hence by definition, accidents cannot be primary beings
Aristotle denies that accidents exist at all
Accidents and substances are interchangeable terms with identical meanings
B7C15.explanation: Aristotle's fundamental point is that an accident, by definition, belongs to something else (a substance) and is not itself the subject of predication. Substance is the subject; accidents are what is predicated of it.

B7C15.q: What role does Aristotle assign to matter in grounding the difference between particular substances?
options: Matter plays no role whatsoever in distinguishing particulars

Matter is what individuates substances; since different portions of matter are numerically distinct, the matter of one human differs from the matter of another, making each particular a distinct substance while sharing the same form
Form alone individuates substances, and matter is irrelevant to numerical distinction
Only immaterial substances are truly individuated; material substances are indistinguishable from one another
B7C15.explanation: Aristotle argues that while form is what makes a thing the kind of thing it is (all humans share the form of humanity), matter is what individuates—different parcels of matter make for different individuals of the same species.

B7C16.q: In Book VII, Chapter 16, how does Aristotle respond to the Platonic claim that universal Forms are the true substances?
options: He fully accepts the Platonic theory and incorporates it into his own system

He rejects it, arguing that if Forms existed separately from sensible particulars, they could not explain how particulars are the beings we actually know; the truly primary substances are concrete individuals (this man, this horse), which possess form and matter together
He claims Forms are substances but exist in the mind alone, not in reality
He argues that only abstract Forms are substances, while concrete particulars are illusory
B7C16.explanation: Aristotle's critique of Platonism is that if Forms were separate substances, they could not explain or cause the being of sensible particulars, which are what we actually know and experience. The primary substances must be the concrete particulars we know.

B7C16.q: According to Aristotle, why is the unity of a substance (e.g., a human being) not the same as the unity of a mere collection or aggregate (e.g., a pile of stones)?
options: There is no difference; collections and individual substances have identical unity

A substance has organic unity where form organizes all parts into a functioning whole directed toward a single end; a collection is merely parts together without such formal organization or purposive unity
Collections have greater unity than substances because they contain more parts
Aristotle treats collections and substances as completely unrelated concepts
B7C16.explanation: Aristotle emphasizes that a substance is a single, unified being through the organizing power of form, whereas a mere collection is just parts placed together without real organic unity. This distinction underlies why a substance is a 'this' but a collection is not.

B7C16.q: What does Aristotle conclude about the nature of substance by the end of Book VII?
options: Substance is finally shown to be purely immaterial and eternal

Substance is the concrete individual thing possessing form and matter together, where form is the essential principle and matter is the individualizing principle; understanding substance is the key to all philosophical inquiry
Substance is revealed to be a purely linguistic convention with no real basis
Substances do not actually exist; only accidents exist
B7C16.explanation: Aristotle's conclusion is that substance is the primary reality, exemplified in concrete individuals unified by form and matter, and that grasping the nature of substance is the answer to the fundamental metaphysical question 'What is being?'

B7C17.q: In Book VII, Chapter 17, what does Aristotle argue about the status of eternal and imperishable substances versus generated and perishable ones?
options: All substances are equally eternal and imperishable

Eternal, imperishable substances (like the heavens and divine intellect) are more truly substances and more knowable in their nature; generated, perishable substances (like animals and plants) are substances but of a lower order
Generated substances are more real than eternal ones because they involve change
There is no meaningful distinction between eternal and generated substances
B7C17.explanation: Aristotle ranks eternal, unchanging substances as more truly substances because they achieve fullness of being without potentiality or change. Generated substances, though genuine substances, exhibit a lower grade of substantiality due to their dependence on matter and potentiality.

B7C17.q: How does Aristotle's discussion of form and matter in Book VII culminate in pointing toward a highest substance that is purely form?
options: Aristotle abandons the form/matter framework entirely at the conclusion

By showing that form is more truly substance than matter, and that an eternal substance would have no matter and potentiality, Aristotle suggests the necessity of a highest substance that is pure form without matter—pointing to what will be developed as the unmoved mover in Book XII
Aristotle denies the existence of any pure form
The highest substance is shown to be pure matter
B7C17.explanation: Aristotle's analysis of form and matter in Book VII establishes the conceptual framework for later arguing that the highest, most necessary reality must be pure form without any material element or potentiality—the divine intellect.

B7C17.q: What methodological lesson does Aristotle draw from his investigation of substance in Book VII about the nature of philosophical inquiry itself?
options: Philosophy should abandon the study of substance as ultimately unknowable

The investigation of substance shows that understanding being requires careful analysis of how terms are used in multiple but related ways; metaphysics proceeds by examining these analogies and resolving puzzles (aporiai) through refined conceptual frameworks
Philosophy has no proper method and cannot make genuine progress
Only mathematical inquiry has any claim to truth; substance is beyond rational investigation
B7C17.explanation: Book VII exemplifies Aristotle's philosophical method: posing puzzles, examining earlier views, distinguishing senses of terms (like 'substance'), and building a comprehensive framework. This methodological lesson guides how metaphysics should proceed.

B12C1.q: In Book XII, Chapter 1, what is Aristotle's opening claim about the relationship between the investigation of substance and the investigation of change or motion?
options: Motion and substance are entirely unrelated subjects requiring separate sciences

The investigation of substance must address how motion and change occur, since motion is a fundamental feature of the natural world and understanding substance requires explaining how things can undergo change
Motion is impossible and therefore not a proper subject of metaphysics
Substance and motion are identical concepts
B12C1.explanation: Aristotle begins Book XII by grounding his investigation of motion in the prior inquiry into substance, establishing that metaphysics must account for how change occurs in the world.

B12C1.q: According to Aristotle, what is the primary puzzle regarding motion (kinesis)?
options: Motion is purely illusory and does not actually exist

Motion requires explanation because change seems to involve becoming from non-being, yet non-being cannot be a source or subject of change; understanding motion requires grasping how potentiality differs from non-being
Motion affects only immaterial things, not physical substances
There is no puzzle about motion; it is immediately evident and needs no explanation
B12C1.explanation: Aristotle's central puzzle is that motion appears to involve something coming from what-is-not, yet genuine non-being cannot underlie change. The solution lies in the act/potency distinction: potential being is real, providing a ground for change.

B12C1.q: What does Aristotle conclude about the necessity of examining all categories in relation to motion?
options: Motion occurs only in the category of substance, not in the other categories
Motion can occur in all categories—there is alteration in quality, growth/diminution in quantity, and change of place in location; these must all be examined to understand motion completely
Motion is impossible in any category and therefore need not be examined
Only in the category of relation can motion occur
B12C1.explanation: Aristotle distinguishes different types of change affecting different categories: alteration (quality), growth/diminution (quantity), locomotion (place), and generation/corruption (substance), establishing that motion pervades multiple categories.

B12C2.q: In Book XII, Chapter 2, what is Aristotle's main argument against the possibility of an infinite regress of movers?
options: An infinite regress is perfectly possible and causes no logical problem

In a series of movers, if each mover moves only because it is moved by another, going back infinitely yields no first mover; but motion must have a source—something that causes motion without itself being moved—so an unmoved mover must exist
Infinite regress is impossible only in the realm of mathematics, not in the physical world
Aristotle accepts infinite regress as inevitable and consistent with his philosophy
B12C2.explanation: Aristotle's teleological argument: a causal series that causes motion cannot extend infinitely backward. Since motion is a fact, there must be a first unmoved mover that initiates and sustains all motion.

B12C2.q: According to Aristotle, what must be true of the unmoved mover in order for it to cause motion in the cosmos without itself moving?
options: The unmoved mover must be material and undergo constant change
The unmoved mover must be an eternal actuality, unmoving and unchanging; it moves other things by being the object of desire and love, not by being moved itself
The unmoved mover must be purely potential, never actualized
Aristotle claims the unmoved mover causes motion through physical contact and impact
B12C2.explanation: Aristotle argues that the unmoved mover acts not through being moved but through being loved or desired—as 'the object of appetite and thought,' it draws things toward itself as the ultimate end, causing motion without undergoing motion.

B12C2.q: What characteristics must the unmoved mover possess according to Aristotle's argument in this chapter?
options: It must be material and subject to decay like everything else in the universe
It must be eternal (without beginning or end), immaterial (without body), indivisible, and incapable of change or motion; it must be pure actuality with no unrealized potential
It must have limited power, affecting only small portions of the cosmos
It must be composed of matter and form like all other substances
B12C2.explanation: Aristotle deduces that an unmoved mover causing eternal motion must itself be eternal, immaterial, immutable, and pure actuality—characteristics required by its necessary role in grounding all motion and change.

B12C3.q: In Book XII, Chapter 3, what does Aristotle argue about the nature of the unmoved mover's activity or life?
options: The unmoved mover is completely inactive and does nothing
The unmoved mover's activity is thinking (noesis); it thinks eternally upon itself, and this self-thinking is the fullness of its perfect actuality—a thinking upon thinking
The unmoved mover creates the world through external actions and commands
The unmoved mover is an inanimate force with no consciousness or activity
B12C3.explanation: Aristotle identifies the unmoved mover's eternal activity as pure intellection directed upon itself. This self-thinking constitutes its perfect actuality and explains how it moves others through being the ultimate object of desire.

B12C3.q: According to Aristotle, what is the object of the unmoved mover's thought?
options: The unmoved mover thinks about changing, perishable things

The unmoved mover thinks about itself—it is both the thinker and the object of thought; its intellection is a thinking-about-thinking, taking itself as its object since it is the most divine and precious thing
The unmoved mover does not think about anything in particular
The unmoved mover thinks about human affairs and mundane concerns
B12C3.explanation: Aristotle emphasizes that the divine intellect thinks eternally upon itself, and this self-directed thinking constitutes its perfection. It is simultaneously the thinker and the object of thought.

B12C3.q: What role does Aristotle assign to the unmoved mover in sustaining the eternal order of the cosmos?
options: The unmoved mover has no role in sustaining the cosmos; it is merely an abstract principle

The unmoved mover sustains cosmic motion by being the eternal object of desire; all things move in the desire to imitate or approach the divine actuality, making the unmoved mover the source and goal of all becoming
The unmoved mover actively pushes or mechanically drives each part of the cosmos
The unmoved mover creates the cosmos in time but then ceases to have any further influence
B12C3.explanation: Aristotle describes how the unmoved mover causes motion throughout the cosmos by being the supreme object of desire; the cosmos eternally imitates and strives toward the divine perfection, finding its source and end in the unmoved mover.

B12C4.q: In Book XII, Chapter 4, how does Aristotle structure the hierarchical relationship between the unmoved mover and other separate substances?
options: There is only one separate substance; all others are dependent on matter

There are multiple separate substances (unmoved movers) corresponding to the revolutions of each celestial sphere, arranged in a hierarchy with the primary unmoved mover at the summit; these eternal intelligences generate motion in the heavens by being the objects of their respective spheres' desire
All separate substances are equal in power and have no hierarchical relationship
Aristotle denies the existence of any separate substances beyond the material cosmos
B12C4.explanation: Aristotle posits a hierarchy of eternal, immaterial substances: the primary unmoved mover and a series of secondary unmoved movers corresponding to the celestial spheres. Each is the object of motion for its respective sphere.

B12C4.q: What does Aristotle say about the relationships and interactions among the multiple unmoved movers in his cosmology?
options: The unmoved movers are in constant communication and dispute with one another

Each unmoved mover is a self-thinking intelligence eternally contemplating itself or a higher principle; the unity of the cosmos derives from their ordered subordination to the primary unmoved mover, each perfect in its own way
The unmoved movers have no relationship to one another whatsoever
The unmoved movers are constantly interfering with each other's motions, causing disorder
B12C4.explanation: Aristotle presents a cosmos with multiple eternal substances arranged in hierarchical order, each possessing the same type of perfect self-thinking activity, yet subordinated to the primary unmoved mover.

B12C4.q: How does Aristotle's account of separate substances relate to his rejection of the Platonic Form of the Good?
options: Aristotle adopts Plato's Form of the Good unchanged

Unlike Plato's transcendent Form of the Good (which is separate from the world it explains), Aristotle grounds being in concrete separate substances—eternal intelligences—that eternally actual and serve as the source and goal of all motion, providing the explanation Plato sought through his Forms
Aristotle rejects both Platonic Forms and the existence of separate substances
Aristotle treats the Form of the Good as identical to the primary unmoved mover
B12C4.explanation: Aristotle's separate substances provide an alternative to Plato's transcendent Form of the Good: rather than a abstract single principle outside the cosmos, Aristotle grounds reality in multiple eternal actualities that explain motion and order through their eternal perfection.

B12C5.q: In Book XII, Chapter 5, what is the significance of Aristotle's claim that the unmoved mover exists 'necessarily'?
options: The unmoved mover exists by chance or coincidence like everything else

The unmoved mover's existence is necessary and not dependent on any external cause; it must necessarily exist because its essence is to be eternally actual, unlike contingent creatures whose existence depends on causes beyond themselves
Necessity means the unmoved mover is subject to constraint and compulsion
The unmoved mover's necessity is merely hypothetical, depending on prior assumptions
B12C5.explanation: Aristotle identifies the unmoved mover as a necessary being whose existence requires no external cause. Its necessity consists in the eternal actuality of its being, making it the source of necessity for all dependent, contingent things.

B12C5.q: How does Aristotle use the distinction between being-by-necessity and contingent being to establish the primacy of the unmoved mover?
options: He argues that all beings are equally contingent and none is necessary

He argues that since the cosmos exhibits order and motion, there must exist something that is necessarily what it is (the unmoved mover); all other things are beings whose existence depends on causes and thus are contingent, making the necessary being primary and the source of all contingent beings
He claims that contingent beings are more fundamental than necessary beings
He denies that necessity applies to any being at all
B12C5.explanation: Aristotle establishes a hierarchy of being: at the summit stands the unmoved mover, necessary in itself; all other beings depend on causes and are contingent. This hierarchy grounds the order of the cosmos.

B12C5.q: What does Aristotle mean when he says the unmoved mover is the 'cause of the being of other things'?
options: The unmoved mover creates other things by an act of will in time

The unmoved mover is the eternal ground and object of desire that actualizes potential beings, drawing all things toward itself as their ultimate perfection; without the unmoved mover as the supreme actuality, other things would lack their ultimate source and goal
The unmoved mover mechanically produces all other beings through efficient causation
Other things are causes of the unmoved mover's being, not vice versa
B12C5.explanation: Aristotle understands causation not as mechanistic production but as the eternal being of the supreme reality that grounds and draws all else toward itself, making the unmoved mover the ultimate source of the being and order of all things.

B12C6.q: In Book XII, Chapter 6, what does Aristotle argue about the nature of knowledge possessed by the divine intellect (the unmoved mover)?
options: The divine intellect has only limited knowledge of certain things but remains ignorant of others

The divine intellect eternally knows all things in their infinite perfection and necessity; through its eternal self-thinking, it possesses perfect knowledge without the imperfection of becoming, without need, without discursive reasoning
The divine intellect does not know anything; it is purely passive
The divine intellect's knowledge is limited to only itself and is ignorant of the rest of reality
B12C6.explanation: Aristotle characterizes the divine intellect as possessing complete, eternal knowledge of all things as they are in their necessary essences, achieved through a single, eternal act of thought rather than through discursive reasoning.

B12C6.q: How does Aristotle reconcile the eternity of divine knowledge with the apparent contingency of future events in the sublunary world?
options: He accepts that divine knowledge makes all future events necessary, eliminating free choice

He argues that the divine intellect, in eternally thinking the necessary principles and essences of all things, knows all that must necessarily be as well as all possible contingencies; what appears contingent to us is known eternally in the divine intellect as part of the eternal order of being
He denies that God has any knowledge of the future whatsoever
He claims future events are entirely unknown even to the divine intellect
B12C6.explanation: Aristotle maintains that divine eternal knowledge encompasses all things within the eternal structure of being, reconciling God's knowledge with the contingency observed in the natural world—a problem that later theologians would wrestle with extensively.

B12C6.q: What does Aristotle conclude about the relationship between the divine life (the eternal actuality of the unmoved mover) and the human aspiration toward wisdom?
options: The divine life is entirely inaccessible to humans and philosophy is futile

Human wisdom consists in contemplating eternal truths and, in this contemplation, the human intellect participates in the divine intellect's eternal activity; the pursuit of wisdom is the fulfillment of human nature because it mirrors the divine life
Humans should abandon contemplation in favor of practical concerns
The divine life is inferior to human practical activities
B12C6.explanation: Aristotle sees philosophy and contemplation as humanity's highest function because in contemplating eternal truths, the human intellect imitates and participates in the divine intellect's perfect actuality, achieving the highest human good.

B12C7.q: In Book XII, Chapter 7, how does Aristotle address the question of whether there are other eternal substances besides the primary unmoved mover?
options: He denies that any other eternal substances exist

He affirms that besides the primary unmoved mover there are other eternal, immaterial substances corresponding to the celestial spheres; the number of these eternal substances determines the structure of the cosmos
He claims all eternal substances are identical to the primary unmoved mover
He leaves the question entirely open without addressing it
B12C7.explanation: Aristotle posits multiple eternal substances in addition to the primary unmoved mover, grounding the complexity and hierarchy of celestial motions within his cosmological system.

B12C7.q: What is Aristotle's argument for the eternity of the cosmos based on the necessity of the unmoved mover?
options: The cosmos is contingent and may cease to exist at any time

Since the unmoved mover eternally exists and eternally causes motion, and since motion is eternal, the cosmos must be eternal; a cosmos that came into being from non-being would require the unmoved mover to change, which is impossible
Aristotle denies the eternity of the cosmos
The cosmos is eternal only in the distant future, not in the past
B12C7.explanation: Aristotle argues that the eternal, unchanging existence of the unmoved mover entails the eternity of cosmic motion. A cosmos that began in time would require the unmoved mover to change, which contradicts its necessary perfection.

B12C7.q: How does Aristotle's doctrine of the unmoved mover culminate his entire metaphysical system as presented in the Metaphysics?
options: The unmoved mover is an extraneous addition unrelated to the rest of metaphysics

The unmoved mover is the culmination of the entire inquiry: it is the first substance (most fully actual), the first principle (source of all being and motion), and the ultimate object of desire; in it, all earlier doctrines about substance, form, actuality, and causation find their completion and highest expression
The unmoved mover refutes all prior arguments in the Metaphysics
Aristotle abandons metaphysics entirely in favor of the doctrine of the unmoved mover
B12C7.explanation: The unmoved mover represents the culmination of Aristotle's entire metaphysical project: it is the ultimate substance, the fullest actuality, the first cause, and the supreme object of philosophy, unifying and perfecting all prior inquiries.

B13C1.q: In Book XIII, Chapter 1, what is Aristotle's opening concern regarding the nature of mathematical objects?
options: Mathematics is a purely linguistic discipline with no connection to reality

The central puzzle is whether mathematical objects (numbers, lines, surfaces) are substances existing separately from sensible things (as Platonists hold), or whether they exist only as the intelligible structure of sensible things
Aristotle denies that mathematical objects exist in any sense
All mathematical objects are identical to sensible physical objects
B13C1.explanation: Aristotle begins Book XIII by raising the fundamental question: are mathematical objects substances that exist apart from sensible things, or are they abstractions from sensible particulars that exist only through intellection?

B13C1.q: According to Aristotle, what is the crucial difference between the Platonic theory of Forms and the Pythagorean theory of numbers regarding their status as substances?
options: There is no meaningful difference between the theories; they are essentially identical

Plato claims the Forms are separate substances that are the causes of sensible things and are predicated of them, while Pythagoreans claim numbers themselves (not Forms) are substances and that sensible things are composed of numbers, making the two approaches quite different in their explanation of sensible things
Pythagoreans invented the theory of Forms, not Plato
Both theories claim mathematical objects are not substances at all
B13C1.explanation: Aristotle distinguishes Platonic Forms from Pythagorean numbers: Plato treats Forms as separate and explanatory of sensibles, while Pythagoreans treat numbers as the actual constituents of sensible things themselves.

B13C1.q: What does Aristotle argue about the possibility of mathematical objects existing as a third realm between Forms and sensible things?
options: A third realm of mathematical intermediates is necessary and coherent

Positing a third realm of mathematical intermediates (besides Forms and sensibles) multiplies entities without solving the fundamental problems: if such intermediates exist, they raise the same difficulties as Forms do, yet fail to explain sensible things
Mathematical objects cannot exist in any form other than as sensible physical things
Aristotle embraces the existence of mathematical intermediates as the solution to all metaphysical puzzles
B13C1.explanation: Aristotle critiques the postulation of a third realm of mathematical intermediates as creating an unnecessary multiplication of entities that replicates problems without providing benefits.

B13C2.q: In Book XIII, Chapter 2, what is Aristotle's main objection to treating numbers as substances in the Pythagorean or Platonic sense?
options: Numbers are perfect substances that require no criticism

If numbers were separate substances, they could not exist in the infinite multiplicity required to explain the infinite variety of sensible things; moreover, mathematical objects seem to lack the causal efficacy required of true substances—they neither act on nor are acted upon by other things
Numbers have nothing whatsoever to do with substances
All numbers are material and hence cannot be substances
B13C2.explanation: Aristotle argues that substances must be causally efficacious, yet numbers appear inert and inefficacious. This disqualifies them from being genuine substances in the way Forms or individual particulars are.

B13C2.q: According to Aristotle, why is the Platonic appeal to 'participation' or 'imitation' to explain how sensibles relate to Forms equally applicable to mathematical objects?
options: Participation and imitation are entirely distinct concepts that cannot be compared

If Platonists must invoke participation to explain how sensibles are related to Forms, they must make the same move to explain how sensibles are related to mathematical objects if those objects are indeed separate substances; yet the more such separate realms are posited, the more the theory multiplies problematic entities
Aristotle denies that participation applies to Forms but must apply to mathematical objects
Participation is a fully satisfactory explanation that requires no criticism
B13C2.explanation: Aristotle points out the logical consistency problem in postulating separate mathematical objects: if participation explained the relation of sensibles to Forms, it must explain their relation to mathematical objects too, yet this approach seems to compound rather than solve problems.

B13C2.q: What does Aristotle conclude about the proper understanding of mathematical objects and their relation to sensible things?
options: Mathematical objects exist entirely independently of sensible things

Mathematical objects are not separate substances but exist as the intelligible structure of sensible things; we apprehend them through a process of abstraction whereby the intellect considers only the quantitative and structural aspects, setting aside sensible qualities and material differences
Sensible things do not possess any mathematical structure
Mathematics is entirely divorced from reality and concerned only with subjective ideas
B13C2.explanation: Aristotle's solution is that mathematical objects exist within sensible things and are grasped through abstraction—the intellect considers sensible things merely as quantities, ignoring their sensible and material aspects.

B13C3.q: In Book XIII, Chapter 3, what does Aristotle argue about the mode of existence of continuous quantities (magnitudes) like lines and surfaces?
options: Lines and surfaces exist as independently substantial objects separate from bodies

Lines and surfaces exist only as limits or boundaries of bodies; a line is the boundary where planes meet, a plane is where a solid is bounded, and thus these lower-dimensional entities depend on the higher-dimensional solids they bound
Lines and surfaces have no real existence whatsoever
Lines and surfaces are the most fundamental substances from which bodies are composed
B13C3.explanation: Aristotle argues that lower-dimensional mathematical entities (surfaces, lines, points) exist as intelligible principles within bodies rather than as independently existing substances; they are limits or boundaries.

B13C3.q: How does Aristotle address the question of whether a line can be divided infinitely?
options: A line cannot be divided at all

A line can be divided infinitely in the sense that one can always specify a further division point, but there are no actual infinitely small parts—the divisibility is potential, not actual; infinity here means the infinite divisibility of the continuum, not the existence of actual infinite parts
A line consists of infinitely many actual points
The concept of division does not apply to lines
B13C3.explanation: Aristotle distinguishes between infinite divisibility in potentiality and the impossible existence of infinitely many actual parts. A continuum is infinitely divisible in principle, but this does not entail actual infinite division.

B13C3.q: What does Aristotle conclude about the status of the unit (one) and numbers as substances?
options: The unit is the fundamental substance from which all other substances arise

If units and numbers were substances in their own right, they would need their own causes and principles of generation/corruption; yet mathematics does not investigate such things, suggesting units and numbers are not substances but principles derived from or inherent in sensible substances
The unit is purely mental and has no real existence
Numbers are the only true substances; all else is derivative
B13C3.explanation: Aristotle argues that the absence of generation and corruption in mathematics suggests that numbers and units are not substances; rather, they are principles or aspects of substances.

B13C4.q: In Book XIII, Chapter 4, what is Aristotle's critique of the Platonic doctrine that the One and the Dyad (Great-and-Small) are the elements of numbers?
options: He fully endorses this doctrine as completely coherent

He argues that if numbers are generated from the One and the Dyad, then the generation of numbers should follow the same patterns as natural generation; but natural generation proceeds by specific determination from matter (as the sculptor shapes bronze), whereas the Platonic scheme proposes numbers generated from the One and Dyad in a manner that fails to parallel or explain natural process
He denies that numbers exist at all
He claims the One and Dyad are sensible physical objects
B13C4.explanation: Aristotle's objection is that the Platonic generation of numbers from non-material principles fails to parallel or illuminate the generation we observe in nature, suggesting the theory is ad hoc and explanatorily sterile.

B13C4.q: According to Aristotle, why is it problematic for Platonists to posit the Forms themselves as patterns (paradeigmata) that sensible things imitate, when applied to mathematical objects?
options: It is not problematic at all

If Forms are patterns for sensibles to imitate, the same should hold for mathematical objects if they are substantively real; yet mathematical objects seem even more abstract and less causally related to sensibles than Forms, making the appeal to 'patterns' even less intelligible in their case
Mathematical objects cannot imitate anything whatsoever
Aristotle denies the existence of patterns entirely
B13C4.explanation: Aristotle extends his critique of the Form-hypothesis: if participation in Forms is already dubious as an explanatory mechanism, it becomes even more dubious when extended to mathematical objects.

B13C4.q: What does Aristotle argue about the nature of mathematical definition and whether it requires reference to separate mathematical objects?
options: Mathematical definitions require reference to separate, eternally existing mathematical forms

Mathematical definitions can be given of the intelligible properties and structures present in sensible things themselves; we do not need separate mathematical objects as definitions already capture the essential structure within the sensible world
Mathematical definitions are purely arbitrary conventions
Mathematics has no definitions whatsoever
B13C4.explanation: Aristotle argues that mathematical definitions express the intelligible structures of sensible things themselves, eliminating the need for a separate realm of mathematical objects.

B13C5.q: In Book XIII, Chapter 5, what does Aristotle argue about the principle of contradiction as it applies to mathematical objects?
options: The principle of non-contradiction does not apply to mathematics

The principle of non-contradiction applies to mathematical objects just as it applies to sensible things and all being; thus a line cannot both be and not be; a number cannot be both odd and even simultaneously
Mathematical objects alone are exempt from the principle of contradiction
The principle of contradiction is merely a convention in mathematics, not a necessary truth
B13C5.explanation: Aristotle extends the principle of non-contradiction universally: it applies to all beings, including mathematical objects, as the fundamental principle of intelligibility.

B13C5.q: How does Aristotle respond to the Platonic claim that Form of Mathematical Objects provides the unifying principle that makes mathematics possible?
options: He accepts the claim fully as the correct explanation

He argues that if a unified mathematical science is possible, it requires a unified subject matter—but invoking separate Forms of each mathematical kind multiplies rather than unifies that subject matter; the unifying principle lies rather in the intelligible structure present within sensible things
He denies that mathematics is a unified science at all
He claims mathematics has no subject matter whatsoever
B13C5.explanation: Aristotle rejects the Platonic solution as counterproductive: it multiplies entities rather than providing unification. True unity comes from grasping the intelligible mathematical structure within the sensible world.

B13C5.q: What is Aristotle's conclusion about the relationship between mathematics and natural science at the end of Book XIII?
options: Mathematics and natural science are entirely unrelated disciplines

Mathematics and natural science are distinct but intimately related: mathematics studies the intelligible structures abstracted from sensible things (quantity, figure, magnitude), while natural science studies those same sensible things in their full concreteness; mathematics is more precise but natural science is more fundamental
Natural science is merely a branch of mathematics
Mathematics is superior to natural science and should replace it
B13C5.explanation: Aristotle delineates the proper relationship: mathematics and natural science are distinct enterprises but related through their common subject—sensible substances—grasped at different levels of abstraction.

B13C6.q: In Book XIII, Chapter 6, what does Aristotle say about the possibility of 'ideal' or 'intermediate' numbers existing as eternal, unchanging mathematical entities?
options: Such ideal numbers definitely exist as the perfect examples of numerical reality

Positing ideal mathematical numbers leads to the same problems as positing Forms: if they exist separately, how do they relate to sensible numbers? If they do not exist separately, the theory is unmotivated; moreover, mathematics does not investigate their generation or destruction, suggesting they are not genuine substances
Ideal numbers are impossible in principle
All numbers are ideal numbers existing in isolation from sensible things
B13C6.explanation: Aristotle extends his criticism to ideal numbers: they face the same problems as Forms, with no clear explanatory advantage, and are ruled out by the fact that mathematics does not concern itself with their coming-to-be or passing-away.

B13C6.q: According to Aristotle, why do Platonists feel compelled to posit a third realm of mathematical intermediates in addition to Forms and sensibles?
options: Because sensible particulars and Forms together provide a complete explanation of all reality

Because sensibles are infinite in number and particular, so their principles must be limited; Forms are eternal and universal; mathematical intermediates seem needed as an intermediate level of being that explains how finite, eternal Forms relate to infinite, particular sensibles
Because Aristotle himself endorsed this theory
Because mathematics makes no sense unless intermediate objects exist
B13C6.explanation: Aristotle reconstructs the Platonic reasoning: intermediates are posited to bridge the explanatory gap between transcendent eternal Forms and the infinite multiplicity of perishable sensibles.

B13C6.q: What methodological principle does Aristotle establish in his critique of mathematical ontologies (Platonism and Pythagoreanism)?
options: One should multiply entities without limit to explain all phenomena

When positing principles or entities to explain phenomena, one should avoid unnecessary multiplication; if sensible things contain intelligible structure, one need not posit separate intelligible objects; abstraction and analysis of existing things are preferable to positing new realms of being
Mathematical theories are immune from criticism because they are 'exact'
Physics and metaphysics have no connection to mathematics
B13C6.explanation: Aristotle's critique establishes a principle of parsimony: existing things are sufficient to ground mathematics through abstraction; separate mathematical realms multiply entities unnecessarily.

B14C1.q: In Book XIV, Chapter 1, what is Aristotle's overall assessment of the theories he has examined that posit principles beyond sensible substance?
options: All such theories are clearly correct and require no criticism

Such theories face difficulties: those who posit eternal, non-sensible principles (Forms, numbers) cannot adequately explain how these relate to or cause sensible things; moreover, they multiply entities without clear necessity; sensible substance itself remains the most comprehensible subject
All theories about non-sensible principles are meaningless
The only correct view is that no principles beyond sensible things exist
B14C1.explanation: Aristotle synthesizes his critique: theories positing transcendent principles are problematic precisely because they cannot adequately explain the known sensible world from which they abstracts or derive.

B14C1.q: According to Aristotle, why does the investigation of being qua being naturally lead one to examine questions about principles and elements?
options: Principles and elements have nothing to do with being as being

To understand what being is, one must investigate what are the first and most fundamental principles from which all things are composed and to which all things reduce; the inquiry into the structure of being naturally unfolds into inquiry into its primary elements and causes
Being as being is entirely independent of any principles or elements
Aristotle denies that principles or elements exist
B14C1.explanation: Aristotle shows how metaphysical inquiry develops logically: understanding being requires understanding the principles that constitute all beings.

B14C1.q: What does Aristotle conclude about the relationship between substance (ousia) and unity (hen) in Book XIV, Chapter 1?
options: Substance and unity are completely unrelated concepts with no meaningful connection

Substance and unity are coextensive or interchangeable: to say something is (has being/substance) is to say it is one; they are the two ways of expressing the same fundamental reality—whatever exists is unified and singular
Substance exists but unity does not
Unity is more fundamental than substance
B14C1.explanation: Aristotle establishes that being and unity are coterminous: every being is one, and every one is a being. They are complementary aspects of the same reality.

B14C2.q: In Book XIV, Chapter 2, how does Aristotle address the ancient puzzle about whether all things are one?
options: He accepts the conclusion that all things are literally one undifferentiated being

He rejects as absurd the conclusion that all things are one; distinction and multiplicity are real; what is one is not all things. Yet he acknowledges that monists perceived a real truth: that all beings share the property of being (they participate in a common nature) and are unified in being, even if they are distinct in their particular natures
He claims the puzzle has no coherent meaning
He accepts that all things are one but denies this conclusion matters
B14C2.explanation: Aristotle refutes actual monism while acknowledging that monists grasped something true: the unity of being. But unity of being does not entail literal identity of all things.

B14C2.q: What does Aristotle say about the distinction between 'being one' and 'being uniform' or 'undifferentiated'?
options: Being one and being undifferentiated are identical concepts

A thing can be one (unified, a single whole) without being undifferentiated; a human being is one unified substance despite having many parts and properties; unity of being is compatible with internal differentiation
Things cannot be unified if they are differentiated
Aristotle never addresses this distinction
B14C2.explanation: Aristotle distinguishes genuine unity (integration of parts into a whole) from undifferentiation (absence of parts or properties). A substance can be one and complex.

B14C2.q: According to Aristotle, what role does form play in generating the unity of a composite substance?
options: Form plays no role in unity; matter alone accounts for unity

Form is the principle of unity for composite things: form organizes the diverse parts and properties of matter into a single, functioning whole; without form's organizing activity, matter would be a mere heap of parts lacking genuine unity
Form destroys unity by introducing differentiation
Unity is entirely independent of form and matter
B14C2.explanation: Aristotle emphasizes that form is the source of unity in substances: it integrates matter and parts into an intelligible, functional whole.

B14C3.q: In Book XIV, Chapter 3, what does Aristotle argue about the principles of being in relation to the principles of substance?
options: The principles of being are entirely distinct from the principles of substance

The principles of being are the same as the principles of substance: form and matter are principles both of substance (qua sensible composite) and of being itself (qua whatness and substratum); studying the principles of being ultimately requires understanding form and matter
Substance has no principles at all
Being has principles, but substance does not
B14C3.explanation: Aristotle argues that the fundamental principles operative in explaining being are the same as those operative in explaining substance—form and matter.

B14C3.q: What is Aristotle's conclusion about whether elements of definition are the same as elements (material constituents) of things?
options: Elements of definition are identical to material elements; there is no distinction

Elements of definition (the genus and specific difference making up the formula) are different from material elements (bronze, wood, etc.), yet both are called 'elements' because both are primary and into which a thing is resolved; definitional elements resolve at the level of essence, material elements at the level of composition
Only one kind of element exists
Elements neither of definition nor of material composition exist
B14C3.explanation: Aristotle makes a crucial distinction: elements can be understood in multiple ways—as definitive principles (genus, differentia) or as material constituents—and both deserve the name 'element' because both are primary components.

B14C3.q: According to Aristotle, why are act and potency counted among the principles of all things?
options: Act and potency are not principles at all

Act and potency are fundamental principles because all change, motion, and the existence of composite beings involve the actualization of potential; distinguishing what is merely potential from what is actual is essential to understanding any being or becoming
Only act is a principle; potency is not
Aristotle denies the importance of the act/potency distinction
B14C3.explanation: Aristotle establishes act/potency as universal principles: understanding any being requires grasping what actualizes the potential, making this distinction fundamental to metaphysics.

B14C4.q: In Book XIV, Chapter 4, what does Aristotle argue about whether the principles of being must be limited in number or could be infinite?
options: There could be infinitely many principles of being

The principles of being cannot be infinite in number; if they were, being itself would be unknowable and science impossible; moreover, infinite principles would not unify reality but fragment it, so being must reduce to a limited number of fundamental principles
The number of principles is arbitrary and makes no difference to philosophy
Aristotle denies that being has principles at all
B14C4.explanation: Aristotle argues that intelligibility requires reducing multiplicity to unity; infinite principles would defeat this purpose, so being must ultimately reduce to a limited set of fundamental principles.

B14C4.q: What does Aristotle say about the ancient Eleatic claim that only one principle (the One) exists?
options: The Eleatic view is obviously correct

The Eleatic view fails because it cannot account for the obvious diversity and multiplicity in nature; if only one principle existed without differentiation, nothing but that one principle would be; yet we observe many distinct beings, requiring principles of differentiation (like the dyad or contrariety)
Aristotle fully endorses monism
The Eleatic view is meaningless
B14C4.explanation: Aristotle refutes monism by pointing out that it cannot account for the fact of multiplicity in nature, showing that principles of differentiation as well as unity are necessary.

B14C4.q: According to Aristotle, how do contraries function as principles in explaining the diversity of being?
options: Contraries are not principles at all

Contraries (like hot/cold, being/non-being in the sense of privation) serve as principles of differentiation; many beings arise from the actualization of contraries, making contrariety a fundamental explanatory principle alongside the principles of unity and substrate
All beings are contraries
Contraries are incapable of being principles
B14C4.explanation: Aristotle includes contraries among the principles because differentiation in nature is often understood through contrary determinations applied to a common substrate.

B14C5.q: In Book XIV, Chapter 5, what is Aristotle's overall conclusion about how to understand the unity and diversity of being?
options: Being is completely unified with no real diversity whatsoever

Being exhibits a complex unity that encompasses genuine diversity: all beings participate in the common nature of being, yet differ in their particular essences and modes; unity and multiplicity coexist through the structure of form, matter, and the actualization of potentials
Being is purely multiple with no real unity
The question of unity and diversity is meaningless
B14C5.explanation: Aristotle synthesizes his investigation: being is genuinely one in nature yet genuinely multiple in its determinations—a conclusion that defines the entire metaphysical project.

B14C5.q: What does Aristotle argue about the relationship between God (the unmoved mover) and the rest of creation in his final synthesis?
options: God is entirely separate and unrelated to creation

God, as the supreme actuality and first principle, is the eternal source and goal of all being; all other beings derive their actuality from eternal participation in and striving toward the divine perfection; this establishes a cosmic hierarchy unified by the divine as the supreme being
Creation and God are identical
Aristotle denies the existence of God
B14C5.explanation: Aristotle's culminating vision: God is the supreme unity and actuality from which all derivative beings flow, establishing the metaphysical basis for understanding how the many proceed from the One.

B14C5.q: What is the ultimate significance of metaphysics as first philosophy according to Aristotle's conclusion in Book XIV?
options: Metaphysics has no practical significance

Metaphysics is the science of being qua being, investigating the first principles and causes of all things; in achieving wisdom about the divine and the eternal principles grounding reality, metaphysics fulfills the highest human aspiration and provides the foundation for all other knowledge
Metaphysics is merely an optional intellectual exercise
Aristotle denies that metaphysics is a genuine science
B14C5.explanation: Aristotle's final statement: metaphysics achieves wisdom in understanding the ultimate principles of being, culminating in the knowledge of God, which represents the fulfillment of human intellectual nature.

B12C7.q: In Book XII, Chapter 7, what does Aristotle argue about whether the form (eidos) of a natural thing is eternal or generated?
options: Forms are generated and perish like individual substances

The form or species itself is eternal and unchangeable; while individual instances come into being and pass away, the specific form or essence persists eternally as the principle from which new individuals are generated
Aristotle denies that forms are eternal
Only matter is eternal; forms are generated
B12C7.explanation: Aristotle maintains that while particular substances are generated and perishable, the forms or species are eternal principles from which generated things arise and to which they return.

B12C7.q: How does Aristotle address the question of whether the unmoved mover's causation is instantaneous or gradual?
options: The unmoved mover causes all motion through a gradual temporal process

The unmoved mover's causation is eternal and unchanging; it moves the cosmos not through temporal action but through being the eternal object of desire that all things eternally seek to imitate, making the motion of the cosmos itself eternal
The unmoved mover's effects occur at random intervals
Causation by the unmoved mover is instantaneous at a single moment in time
B12C7.explanation: Aristotle's unmoved mover operates through eternal presence as the eternal object of aspiration, not through temporal causation, grounding the eternity of cosmic motion.

B12C7.q: What does Aristotle conclude about the scope of the unmoved mover's knowledge and causal efficacy?
options: The unmoved mover knows only itself and has no causal influence on the cosmos

The unmoved mover, through its eternal self-thinking, eternally 'knows' all things in their necessary essences and principles; this eternal knowledge grounds the intelligible order of the cosmos, and the mover's perfection serves as the ultimate cause and goal that gives all motion and being their direction and meaning
The unmoved mover knows nothing at all
The unmoved mover's knowledge is limited to sensible, changing things
B12C7.explanation: Aristotle emphasizes that the divine intellect's eternal knowledge of eternal principles is both perfectly self-contained and eternally productive of cosmic order.

B12C8.q: In Book XII, Chapter 8, what is Aristotle's response to the question of whether pleasure or happiness characterizes the life of the unmoved mover?
options: The unmoved mover is devoid of pleasure or happiness

The unmoved mover achieves the highest pleasure and happiness through its eternal self-thinking; contemplation of the most perfect object (itself) at every moment constitutes supreme actuality and perfect felicity, and this divine life of eternal contemplation is the model for human flourishing
Pleasure and happiness are inferior to the unmoved mover's nature
The unmoved mover experiences constant suffering
B12C8.explanation: Aristotle argues that the unmoved mover's eternal contemplation of eternal truth is the fullness of happiness and pleasure—it lacks nothing and achieves perpetual perfection.

B12C8.q: How does Aristotle compare the eternal self-thinking of the unmoved mover to human contemplation and theoretical wisdom?
options: Human contemplation is inferior to divine thinking in every respect with no common ground

Human theoretical wisdom, while finite and discursive, imitates the structure of divine self-thinking; in contemplating eternal truths, the human intellect approximates the divine intellect's eternal activity, achieving its highest good through participation in divinity
Divine and human thinking are identical
Human contemplation has no relation to the divine intellect
B12C8.explanation: Aristotle establishes a continuity: human wisdom participates in and mirrors the divine intellect's eternal activity, giving human philosophical contemplation its ultimate significance.

B12C8.q: What does Aristotle say about the question of whether the unmoved mover creates the world or whether the world exists eternally?
options: The unmoved mover creates the world from nothing at a specific moment in time

Since the unmoved mover is eternal and eternally actual, and since motion is eternal, the cosmos must exist eternally; creation in time is impossible because it would require the unmoved mover to change, contradicting its perfection; rather, eternal motion derives eternally from eternal actuality
The world is created and will eventually cease to exist
Aristotle claims the unmoved mover did not create the world
B12C8.explanation: Aristotle's metaphysics implies eternal creation: the cosmos flows eternally from the eternal divine actuality, not from a temporal act of creation.

B12C9.q: In Book XII, Chapter 9, what does Aristotle establish about the relationship between the unmoved mover and the structure of the cosmos?
options: The unmoved mover has no connection to the cosmos's structure

The unmoved mover, as the eternal object of desire for all things, establishes the order and unity of the cosmos; each level of being—from pure matter through celestial spheres to God—is arranged hierarchically with all things oriented toward the divine perfection, making the cosmos a unified system of subordination to the unmoved mover
The cosmos is structured independently of any divine principle
The unmoved mover disrupts cosmic order rather than establishing it
B12C9.explanation: Aristotle shows how the unmoved mover, though inactive in the strict sense, orders the entire cosmos by being the ultimate object of all desire and striving.

B12C9.q: How does Aristotle respond to the apparent paradox that the unmoved mover influences an eternal cosmos without itself undergoing any change?
options: He denies that any influence is possible without change

He resolves it by distinguishing between causation by efficient action (which requires change) and causation by being the object of desire (which requires no change); the unmoved mover moves all things not by doing something but by being the eternal end toward which all things eternally aim
He accepts the paradox as ultimately irresolvable
He claims the cosmos is not truly influenced by the unmoved mover
B12C9.explanation: Aristotle's solution rests on distinguishing causal modes: the unmoved mover causes motion not as an efficient agent but as a final cause—as the eternal telos toward which all motion aims.

B12C9.q: What is the ultimate metaphysical principle that Aristotle establishes through his analysis of the unmoved mover and the cosmos?
options: Matter is the ultimate principle of all reality

Being is fundamentally derived from and oriented toward pure actuality (God); all motion, change, and multiplicity flow from the eternal perfection of the unmoved mover, making divinity the source, goal, and ground of all existence
The cosmos is self-explanatory and requires no ultimate principle
Aristotle abandons the search for ultimate principles
B12C9.explanation: Aristotle's culminating insight: all reality is structured around eternal actuality (divinity) as its source and goal, establishing the metaphysical foundation for understanding all being.

B12C10.q: In Book XII, Chapter 10, what is Aristotle's conclusion about the nature of the divine mind and its relation to the cosmos?
options: The divine mind is unaware of the cosmos and indifferent to its existence

The divine mind, in eternally thinking the eternal essences and principles of all things, knows the cosmos in its eternal structure; this eternal knowledge constitutes both the perfection of the divine intellect and the eternal ground of cosmic intelligibility and order
The divine mind is constantly manipulating and changing the cosmos
The cosmos is unknown even to the divine mind
B12C10.explanation: Aristotle establishes that the divine intellect's eternal self-knowledge encompasses knowledge of all eternal principles, grounding both divine perfection and cosmic order.

B12C10.q: What does Aristotle argue is the true sense in which God is 'providential' or cares for the cosmos, despite not acting or changing?
options: God actively intervenes in worldly affairs constantly

God's providential care consists in eternally embodying the perfect form of being; all things are ordered by their natural orientation toward this divine perfection, and in achieving their own actualization, they participate in divine providence without God needing to act or intervene temporally
God is completely indifferent to the cosmos's existence
Providence is incompatible with God's unchanging nature
